tagline: Where the Sahara meets the Atlantic
overview:
Mauritania stretches across the western Sahara in northwest Africa, with the Atlantic Ocean on one side and Mali and Algeria on the other, and Senegal along its southern river border. It is about one and a half times the size of Texas, but three-quarters of it is desert, and the population is only about 5 million. The capital, Nouakchott, was a small fishing village when it was chosen as capital in 1958 and has since exploded into a sprawling city of more than a million people where sand drifts into the streets.

Arabic is the official language, and Hassaniya Arabic is the everyday speech of most Mauritanians, while Pulaar, Soninke, and Wolof are spoken by peoples in the south; French is widely used in business. Mauritania is an Islamic republic, and essentially all its people are Muslim. Fishing in some of the richest waters in the world, iron ore mining, and herding camels and goats support the economy, and gold and oil have been developed more recently. The country's society is divided between Arab-Berber Moors and Black African communities.
landAndNature: Most of Mauritania is flat Saharan plain of sand and gravel, broken by the sandstone plateaus of the Adrar and Tagant, where old caravan towns sit beside date-palm oases and the Richat Structure, a 40-kilometer ring of rock nicknamed the Eye of the Sahara, is visible from space. Only the Senegal River valley in the far south is green enough for farming. The Atlantic coast is where the desert simply ends in the sea: at Banc d'Arguin National Park, dunes meet shallow waters where more than two million migrating shorebirds gather each winter, one of the greatest bird spectacles on Earth. Dolphins there famously help local Imraguen fishermen drive fish into their nets. Sandstorms, blistering heat, and years without rain shape life in the interior.
peopleAndCulture: Mauritanians are Moors of Arab and Berber descent, both the lighter-skinned Bidhan and the Haratin, descendants of enslaved people, along with Fulani, Soninke, and Wolof peoples of the south. Nomadic traditions live on: families gather in tents on woven rugs to drink three rounds of sweet green tea, and camel racing and milk are prized. Meals feature thieboudienne, rice with fish and vegetables, méchoui, whole roasted lamb, and couscous. Women wear flowing colorful veils called melhfa, and men wear the wide blue or white daraa robe. Griots sing poetry to the tidinit lute and the ardin harp, and the ancient libraries of Chinguetti hold rare manuscripts. Soccer is the leading sport, and the national team reached its first Africa Cup of Nations in 2019.
history: Rock art shows that the Sahara here was once grassland grazed by cattle. Berber tribes controlled the caravan routes, and Chinguetti, founded in the 1200s, became a holy city where pilgrims gathered before crossing the desert to Mecca. The Almoravid movement that conquered Morocco and Spain in the 1000s began in this region. Arab tribes arrived in the 1400s and 1500s and mixed with the Berbers to form the Moors. France took control in the early 1900s. Independence came on November 28, 1960. Mauritania has had several military coups, a war over Western Sahara in the 1970s, and ethnic tensions in 1989. It was the last country in the world to abolish slavery, in 1981, and it made slavery a crime only in 2007, though the practice has not fully ended.
funFacts: The Richat Structure, a 40-kilometer bull's-eye of rock in the desert, is so distinctive that astronauts use it as a landmark.
An iron-ore train in Mauritania is one of the longest in the world, stretching about 2.5 kilometers, and people ride free on top of the ore.
Mauritania was the last country on Earth to abolish slavery, in 1981.
At Banc d'Arguin, wild dolphins help fishermen by herding mullet toward their nets, a partnership going back generations.
Chinguetti's libraries hold Islamic manuscripts up to 800 years old, kept by families in a town slowly being buried by sand.
